item.title: Podcast: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.category: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.description: Jev from TypeSafe AI answers a defined question about text with a probability. What happens when researchers put this unusual tool through cognitive tests designed for people? This short conversation follows the independent work on xanderpico.com: a trait-order result opposite to the first-impression pattern used for comparison, a conjunction judgment that changes with layout, and word-similarity rankings that resemble human ratings while the raw scores do not. The hosts turn those results into practical advice for builders: pin the version and exact question, test wording, order and layout, compare with human ratings where available, and keep inactive inputs separate. The article and linked result write-ups have the full methods, numbers and caveats. Independent work; not affiliated with or endorsed by TypeSafe. This episode uses scripted AI-generated hosts and synthetic voices.

item.title: Results: Which senses does a text-only AI hear in a word?
item.category: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.description: Jev rates 600 words on six senses and two body actions and is compared with human norms: closest on touch, furthest on the inner-body sense. Work in progress.

item.title: Results: Do word pairs feel as similar to Jev as to people?
item.category: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.description: A cheap AI model rates 999 word pairs for similarity and is compared with people's ratings: it ranks them well but is a harsher judge, and the wording of the question matters. Work in progress.

item.title: Article: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies: a short research article
item.category: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.description: A short summary and research article pulling the Jev results together: what a fast, cheap judgment model shares with people, where it differs, and what that means for AI builders, Jev users and brain researchers.

item.title: Thread: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.category: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.description: Where do the quick judgments of a very cheap AI differ from ours, and what does running thousands of tests teach us about minds and about building with AI? Jev, from TypeSafe AI, answers a typed question about a text with a probability in about a fifth of a second for about two thousandths of a cent, and when it is confident it gives the same answer each time. That makes psychology-style experiments practical at a scale that normally needs hundreds of volunteers: rating thousands of words, or running a battery of classic bias tests in minutes. What turns up matters to AI builders, Jev users and brain researchers: some human quirks appear, some do not, and on first impressions it does the opposite of people.

item.title: Results: Rating words the way people do
item.category: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.description: A cheap AI model rates 400 words each for concreteness, valence and arousal and is compared with published human norms: close on two, weaker on arousal, and where it disagrees. Work in progress.

item.title: Results: Eight classic bias tests, one cheap AI model, two cents
item.category: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.description: A battery of classic psychology tests run on a fast, cheap AI judgment model: which human quirks it shows, which it does not, and the one it reverses. Includes the Linda problem and a first-impressions test that comes out the opposite way to people. Work in progress.

item.title: Guide: Building with a gut-feeling model: notes from 200,000 calls
item.category: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.description: Practical rules for using Jev, a fast, cheap AI judgment model, from about 200,000 logged calls, including one failed attempt at a worm's nerve circuit.
